title: SHE DIED, AND THE WIDOWS BROUGHT OUT THEIR CLOTHES—BECAUSE SOME LIVES PREACH EVEN AFTER THEIR LAST BREATH
paragraphs: SHE DIED, AND THE WIDOWS BROUGHT OUT THEIR CLOTHES—BECAUSE SOME LIVES PREACH EVEN AFTER THEIR LAST BREATH
She never needed a pulpit to demonstrate the Gospel. She had a needle, a heart surrendered to Christ, and a room full of grieving women who would soon witness the impossible.
Imagine walking into a room after someone you love has died.
Nobody is talking about how much money she had.
Nobody is mentioning her physical appearance, her social status, her popularity, or how many people knew her name.
Instead, women are crying.
Their trembling hands are holding pieces of clothing.
Every garment carries a memory. Every stitch tells a story. Every piece of fabric bears evidence that someone once cared enough to notice their suffering.
The woman who made them is lying lifeless nearby.
Her name was Tabitha.
And before God would demonstrate His extraordinary power through her resurrection, her life had already demonstrated something that many Christians spend their entire lives struggling to understand.
The Gospel is not merely something we proclaim with our mouths. It is something that should become visible through the way we live.
Acts 9:36 introduces her with remarkable simplicity:
“Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.” — Acts 9:36, KJV
There is something extraordinary hidden within the original Greek text.
Luke describes Tabitha as a μαθήτρια (mathētria), meaning a female disciple. This is the only occurrence of this particular feminine form of the word disciple in the New Testament.
Before Scripture tells us what she made, it tells us whom she followed.
She belonged to Jesus.
Her identity was not rooted in her usefulness, her generosity, or her ability to help others. Her good works flowed from her identity as a disciple of Christ.
Her Aramaic name, טביתא (Ṭabīṯā), and its Greek equivalent, Δορκάς (Dorkas), both mean gazelle.
But what makes her unforgettable is not the beauty of her name.
It is the beauty of a life transformed by the Gospel.
Luke describes her as:
πλήρης ἔργων ἀγαθῶν καὶ ἐλεημοσυνῶν
Plērēs ergōn agathōn kai eleēmosynōn.
Literally, “full of good works and acts of mercy.”
The word plērēs means full. The word eleēmosynē refers to charitable giving or acts of mercy toward those in need.
Compassion was not merely an occasional activity for Tabitha.
It characterized her life.
She did not simply speak about helping people.
She helped them.
She did not merely acknowledge suffering.
She responded to it.
And perhaps this is where her story begins to make us uncomfortable.
Because we live in a generation where it has become remarkably easy to look compassionate without actually sacrificing anything.
We can post Bible verses about generosity while ignoring someone who desperately needs assistance.
We can type “Praying for you” and forget the person before the day ends.
We can sing about surrender on Sunday while refusing to surrender our time, comfort, resources, or pride on Monday.
We can become so concerned about appearing Christian that we forget what following Christ actually looks like.
Tabitha's life confronts that contradiction.
Not because her good works earned her salvation.
Scripture is unmistakably clear about that.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9
But the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
We are not saved by good works. We are saved by grace, and that grace produces good works.
Tabitha was not purchasing God's love through her generosity.
She was demonstrating the love of the God to whom she belonged.
Then something happened that nobody could prevent.
She became sick.
And she died.
Just like that, the woman who had helped others could no longer help herself.
The hands that had made garments became still.
The woman who had brought comfort to others became the reason others were grieving.
Acts 9:37 tells us that her body was washed and placed in an upper room.
Do not rush past that moment.
There is a painful truth here that many believers need to hear.
Faithful Christians still experience suffering.
Generous people still become sick.
People who pray still receive devastating news.
People who love Jesus still experience grief, disappointment, financial hardship, and death.
Tabitha's goodness did not exempt her from mortality.
Her suffering was not evidence that God had abandoned her.
Sometimes we secretly believe that if we serve God faithfully enough, nothing terrible should happen to us.
Then something terrible happens.
And suddenly, we do not know what to do with our faith.
Perhaps you know that feeling.
You prayed.
You served.
You gave what you could.
You tried to remain faithful even when nobody appreciated your sacrifices.
And still, something broke.
Your family.
Your health.
Your finances.
Your relationship.
Your heart.
You found yourself wondering why the God you loved allowed something you never imagined you would have to survive.
Tabitha's story does not give us permission to promise that every tragedy will be reversed in this lifetime.
But it reminds us that suffering does not have the authority to cancel the promises of Jesus Christ.
Death itself will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
When the disciples in Joppa heard that Peter was nearby in Lydda, they sent two men to him, urging him to come without delay.
Peter went.
And when he entered the upper room, something deeply moving happened.
“...and all the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made, while she was with them.” — Acts 9:39
They showed him the clothes.
Think about that.
The evidence of her discipleship was not a collection of impressive religious speeches.
It was something they could hold in their hands.
The Greek text mentions χιτῶνας (chitōnas) and ἱμάτια (himatia), referring to tunics and outer garments or clothing.
These were practical necessities.
In a society where widows could be particularly vulnerable, such acts of provision carried profound significance.
Scripture does not give us the personal history of every widow in that room. But it does tell us enough to understand why their grief was accompanied by visible evidence of Tabitha's kindness.
She had made something that mattered to them.
And now they were holding what remained.
What would people hold up if you were no longer here tomorrow?
Not what would they say at your funeral because politeness demanded it.
What would they genuinely remember?
Would someone remember that you helped them when they had nothing?
Would someone remember that you forgave them when they deserved rejection?
Would your children remember a parent who taught them about Jesus through both words and actions?
Would someone remember that you made them feel seen during the darkest season of their life?
Would someone be closer to Christ because you lived?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But eternity has a way of exposing the things we spend our lives pretending are important.
One day, the possessions we accumulated will belong to someone else.
The compliments we chased will become distant memories.
The arguments we were determined to win will lose their significance.
The online attention we worked so hard to maintain will eventually disappear.
And we will stand before the Lord.
What a tragedy it would be to spend an entire lifetime building a reputation while neglecting the people God placed within our reach.
Tabitha had left behind something more meaningful than an impressive reputation.
She had left behind evidence of mercy.
Then Peter did something important.
He sent everyone out of the room.
He knelt.
And he prayed.
Before he spoke to the dead woman, he spoke to God.
Before the miracle, there was dependence.
Peter understood that resurrection power did not belong to him. He was an apostle, but he was still a servant. The authority belonged to the risen Jesus Christ.
Then, turning toward the body, he said:
Ταβιθά, ἀνάστηθι.
Tabitha, anastēthi.
“Tabitha, arise.”
— Acts 9:40
She opened her eyes.
She saw Peter.
She sat up.
The woman whose death had filled the room with sorrow was alive again.
Peter gave her his hand, lifted her up, and called the believers and widows back into the room.
He presented her alive.
Can you imagine the emotional weight of that moment?
The same women who had entered the room carrying garments and grief were now looking at the woman whose life they had mourned.
What had appeared irreversible had been overturned by the power of God.
There is also a remarkable connection between this passage and an earlier moment in Peter's life.
In Mark 5:41, Jesus raised Jairus's daughter and spoke the Aramaic words:
Ταλιθὰ κούμ — Talitha koum.
“Little girl, I say unto thee, arise.”
Peter had been among the disciples permitted to witness that miracle.
Years later, in Joppa, the similarities are striking.
Talitha.
Tabitha.
But there is a crucial distinction.
Jesus commanded with His own authority.
Peter knelt and prayed before speaking.
The servant depended upon the Lord.
And the miracle in Joppa ultimately pointed beyond Peter, beyond Tabitha, and beyond the grieving widows.
Acts 9:42 reveals the greater purpose:
“And it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord.”
That is the destination of the entire story.
Many believed in the Lord.
Not merely in the power of generosity.
Not in the greatness of Peter.
Not in the goodness of Tabitha.
In the Lord.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people doing extraordinary things.
It is the story of a holy God redeeming sinners through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Tabitha was restored to mortal life. Jesus rose victorious over death, never to die again (Romans 6:9).
Her restoration was a sign of divine power.
His resurrection is the foundation of our eternal hope.
And that changes everything.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a past that makes you feel unqualified to serve God.
Perhaps you have wasted years.
Perhaps you have been selfish, dishonest, unfaithful, bitter, or indifferent to the suffering of others.
Perhaps your life looks nothing like Tabitha's.
You cannot undo every decision you have made.
You cannot recover every opportunity you have wasted.
But you can repent.
You can come to Jesus Christ.
You can receive the forgiveness that you could never earn.
And through His grace, the hands that once caused pain can become hands that bring comfort.
The mouth that once spread gossip can become a voice of encouragement.
The resources once consumed by selfish ambition can become instruments of generosity.
The life once dominated by sin can become a testimony to redemption.
That is what it means to go from scandal to grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not excusing sin.
Not disguising our failures with religious language.
But bringing our brokenness before Jesus, turning away from sin, and allowing His grace to transform the way we live.
You do not need to be famous to serve Christ.
You do not need thousands of followers.
You do not need a microphone, a ministry title, or extraordinary abilities.
Tabitha reminds us that ordinary skills surrendered to an extraordinary Savior can become instruments of genuine ministry.
Your kitchen can become a place of generosity.
Your home can become a place of hospitality.
Your words can become instruments of encouragement.
Your profession can become an opportunity to demonstrate integrity.
Your resources can help carry the Gospel to someone you may never meet.
Never underestimate what God can accomplish through a willing heart.
And never confuse being unnoticed by people with being insignificant before God.
Hebrews 6:10 reminds believers that God is not unjust to forget their work and the love they have shown toward His name through serving others.
The world may never applaud your obedience.
Heaven does not require the world's applause.
Take a moment to pray.
Ask Jesus to reveal where your faith has become comfortable, where your compassion has grown cold, and where your generosity has been replaced by excuses.
You may also share a testimony of someone whose quiet kindness helped you through a difficult season. Their story might encourage another person who feels forgotten today.
Someone may be struggling with their purpose. Someone may believe that their past has permanently disqualified them from being used by God.
This is also the heart behind Gospel Warrior.

We want to reach people beyond the walls of a church building—to bring Scripture into homes, into difficult conversations, into seasons of grief, and into the lives of people who desperately need to rediscover the truth of the Gospel.
But continuing and expanding this work also requires practical support.
Just as Tabitha used what she had to serve others, every believer has opportunities to participate in work that honors Christ.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be a meaningful expression of stewardship, gratitude, and a desire to glorify God.
Grace is freely given through Jesus Christ.

There are many ways to serve.
What matters is that our service flows from love for Jesus rather than a desire to be seen by others.
Because one day, our hands will become still, too.
Someone else will occupy the rooms we once occupied.
Someone else will own the things we once treasured.
Our names may gradually disappear from ordinary conversations.
But the Lord will remain.
And those who belong to Jesus Christ have a hope that reaches beyond the grave.
So while your hands can still move, use them to serve.
While your voice can still speak, use it to proclaim truth.
While your heart can still respond, surrender it to Christ.
While you still have opportunities to give, forgive, encourage, love, and demonstrate mercy, do not continually postpone obedience until tomorrow.
Tabitha's story began with a disciple whose life was full of good works.
It passed through sickness, death, tears, prayer, and miraculous restoration.
And it ended with people believing in the Lord.
May that become the testimony of our lives as well.
Not that people remember how impressive we were.
Not that they build monuments to our generosity.
But that, because of the grace of Jesus made visible through our lives, someone else discovers the Savior.
When your hands can no longer serve and your voice can no longer speak, may the mercy of Christ that flowed through your life still be telling someone where to find Him.
